idiom_name: Task-returning method + async/await, Progress<T> for progress
implementation_notes: The modern realization: the start method returns Task<T> immediately and await suspends the caller without blocking it, resuming when the task completes; failure arrives as a faulted task rather than as an event argument, and Progress<T>/IProgress<T> carry progress callbacks ('provides an IProgress<T> that invokes callbacks for each reported progress value') marshalled to the captured context. EAP remains the legacy event-shaped realization that TAP replaced (Microsoft documents EAP as 'the event-based legacy model for providing asynchronous behavior'); bridge old components with TaskCompletionSource or the documented EAP-to-TAP adapters instead of writing new EAP surfaces.
pitfalls: Blocking on a task that needs the captured SynchronizationContext (task.Wait(), .Result on a UI thread) deadlocks - await instead of waiting.
await resumes on the captured context by default, so ConfigureAwait(false) in a library that then touches UI state resumes on a pool thread and throws.
async void is only for event handlers: its exceptions cannot be awaited or caught by the caller.

variants.name: MethodNameAsync + MethodNameCompleted (classic EAP shape)
variants.implementation_notes: The classic event realization as Microsoft defined it: a start method returns void and raises MethodNameCompleted exactly once with AsyncCompletedEventArgs (Result/Error/Cancelled/UserState), optionally raises progress events and accepts an AsyncCancel request; AsyncOperationManager posts those events to the SynchronizationContext captured at start, which is what makes the component host-agnostic. BackgroundWorker (DoWork/ProgressChanged/RunWorkerCompleted) is the packaged version. Keep this shape only for components that must serve pre-Task hosts or preserve an existing event-based surface.
pitfalls: EAP completion is posted to the SynchronizationContext captured when the operation started; blocking that context (or blocking on a Task wrapping it) deadlocks.
Subscribed handlers are never unsubscribed by the pattern, and per-operation handlers on a long-lived component keep the subscriber alive - EAP's documented leak.
Cancellation is a request: CancelAsync only sets a flag that the DoWork body must poll, and the completion still fires with Cancelled = true.
